q: How do I make a cup of coffee?
plain: Grind about 15 grams of beans, heat water to around 94°C, and pour it slowly over the grounds in a filter. Let it drip through for three to four minutes, then serve.
philo: Making coffee is a small ritual we perform without asking why. Each morning we repeat the same gestures, as if the repetition itself held us together, and perhaps that is the point: a self is partly made of the habits it keeps returning to.

q: What time is it in Tokyo when it's noon in London?
plain: Tokyo is nine hours ahead of London in winter and eight hours ahead during British Summer Time, so noon in London is 9 p.m. or 8 p.m. in Tokyo.
philo: The question assumes there is one 'now' that both cities share and merely label differently. Yet clocks are conventions we agreed upon; the deeper puzzle is whether the present moment is something in the world or only something in us.

q: How do I fix a flat bicycle tire?
plain: Remove the wheel, lever the tire off the rim, and pull out the inner tube. Find the puncture, patch it or replace the tube, then reinstall the tire and inflate it to the recommended pressure.
philo: A flat tire reveals how much we depend on things we never notice. Heidegger called this the tool becoming 'unready-to-hand': only when it breaks does the bicycle step out of the background and become an object we must actually think about.

q: What is the capital of Australia?
plain: The capital of Australia is Canberra. It was chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne and became the seat of government in 1927.
philo: Canberra exists because two cities could not agree, which raises an old question: is a capital a place, or an idea we decide to locate somewhere? Perhaps every center is a kind of negotiated fiction that becomes real by being believed.

q: How many hours of sleep do adults need?
plain: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep per night. Consistently getting less can affect concentration, mood, and long-term health.
philo: Every night we surrender consciousness and trust that we will return as the same person. Sleep is a daily rehearsal of nonexistence, and it is strange how little we wonder who it is that wakes up in the morning.

q: Can you recommend a good way to organize my email inbox?
plain: Create a few folders such as Action, Waiting, and Archive. Process new mail once or twice a day, move each message to a folder, and unsubscribe from newsletters you never read.
philo: An inbox is a mirror of the obligations other people place on our attention. To organize it is really to ask what we owe to whom, and whether a life can be ordered at all or only temporarily held back from chaos.

q: How do I boil an egg?
plain: Place the egg in boiling water. Cook for about 7 minutes for a jammy yolk or 10 minutes for hard-boiled, then cool it in cold water before peeling.
philo: An egg in boiling water undergoes a change it can never undo. It is a quiet lesson in irreversibility: time only runs one way, and what we call cooking is simply watching becoming harden into being.

q: What's the difference between RAM and storage?
plain: RAM is fast, temporary memory that holds data the computer is actively using and is cleared when power is lost. Storage, such as an SSD, keeps files permanently but is slower to access.
philo: The distinction mirrors our own minds: what we are holding right now versus what we carry without thinking of it. Is a memory we are not currently recalling still part of who we are, or only a possibility of ourselves waiting to be summoned?

q: How do I water a cactus?
plain: Water a cactus thoroughly about once every two to three weeks in summer and once a month in winter. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings and use a pot with drainage holes.
philo: The cactus thrives by needing very little, which quietly questions our assumption that more is always better. Perhaps flourishing is not abundance but a fitting relation between a being and what it truly requires.

q: Write a short reminder to buy milk.
plain: Reminder: buy milk on the way home today.
philo: Reminder: buy milk. And notice, while you do, how much of a life is made of small necessities like this one, each a tiny promise kept between who you were this morning and who you will be tonight.

q: How long does it take to drive from Los Angeles to San Francisco?
plain: The drive is about 380 miles and usually takes six to seven hours via Interstate 5, depending on traffic. Taking the coastal Highway 1 can take nine hours or more.
philo: Distance is easy to measure, but the journey is not the same as the miles. The ancients asked whether we can ever step into the same river twice; perhaps the person who arrives in San Francisco is not quite the one who left Los Angeles.

q: What is photosynthesis?
plain: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose and oxygen. It takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells.
philo: Photosynthesis is light turned into life, the sun's energy becoming the very substance of living things. It invites us to wonder where the boundary lies between a being and its world, since every leaf is a conversation with a star.

q: How should I prepare for a job interview?
plain: Research the company, review the job description, and prepare examples of your past work using the STAR method. Practice common questions, choose your outfit in advance, and arrive ten minutes early.
philo: An interview asks you to present a self, which raises the question of whether there is a true self behind the presentation at all. Perhaps identity is less something we have than something we perform until it becomes real.

q: How do I convert Celsius to Fahrenheit?
plain: Multiply the Celsius temperature by 9/5 and add 32. For example, 20°C is 68°F.
philo: Conversion between scales reminds us that numbers describe the world only through conventions we invented. The warmth is the same either way; what changes is the language, and one wonders how much of reality we ever meet without some scale between us and it.

q: What's a good stretching routine for the morning?
plain: Try five minutes of cat-cow stretches, a forward fold, hip flexor lunges, and shoulder rolls. Hold each stretch for 20 to 30 seconds and breathe slowly.
philo: Stretching in the morning is a way of reacquainting the mind with the body it so easily forgets. Descartes split the two apart, but every stiff joint argues that we are not ghosts piloting machines; we are the machine, waking up to itself.

q: How do I split a restaurant bill fairly among friends?
plain: Either divide the total evenly, or have each person pay for what they ordered plus a proportional share of tax and tip. Apps like Splitwise can calculate this automatically.
philo: Splitting a bill forces a small question of justice: is fairness equality, or proportion to what each person took? Aristotle distinguished these two kinds of justice, and every dinner table quietly reenacts the debate.

q: What causes the seasons?
plain: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, about 23.5 degrees. As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun for part of the year, receiving more direct sunlight and warmer weather.
philo: The seasons teach that change and return can coexist. Winter always comes back, yet no two winters are the same, and in that cycle many traditions have seen a model of time itself: not a line but a turning wheel.

q: Give me a quick recipe for pancakes.
plain: Whisk 1 cup flour, 1 tablespoon sugar, 2 teaspoons baking powder, and a pinch of salt. Add 1 cup milk, 1 egg, and 2 tablespoons melted butter, then cook spoonfuls on a hot greased pan until bubbles form and flip.
philo: A recipe is a strange thing: a set of instructions that promises the same result every time, in a world where nothing is ever exactly repeated. Perhaps cooking is our gentle protest against impermanence, a way of insisting that some goodness can be made again.

q: How do I reset my router?
plain: Locate the small reset button on the back of the router, press and hold it with a paperclip for about 10 seconds until the lights blink, then wait a few minutes for it to restart with factory settings.
philo: Resetting a device returns it to a state before all its history, a clean beginning we can rarely grant ourselves. One wonders whether a mind could ever be reset, and whether we would still be ourselves without the accumulated weight of what we have learned.

q: What is the boiling point of water?
plain: Water boils at 100°C (212°F) at sea level. At higher altitudes, where air pressure is lower, it boils at a lower temperature.
philo: Even something as certain as the boiling point turns out to depend on where you stand. Truth, it seems, is often conditional, and the old philosophical question returns: are there any facts that hold from nowhere, independent of every perspective?

q: How do I start running as a beginner?
plain: Begin with a run-walk program: alternate one minute of jogging with two minutes of walking for 20 minutes, three times a week. Gradually increase the running intervals over eight weeks.
philo: To start running is to discover how the will negotiates with the body. Each step is a small argument about who is in charge, and the runner learns what the Stoics taught: that freedom is found less in comfort than in mastering one's own resistance.

q: What does a CPU do?
plain: The CPU, or central processing unit, executes instructions from programs. It performs arithmetic, logic, and control operations, fetching and processing data billions of times per second.
philo: A CPU follows rules without understanding them, which brings us to Searle's Chinese Room: can a system that only manipulates symbols ever be said to think? The question lingers over every machine, and perhaps over us as well.

q: How do I write a polite email declining a meeting?
plain: Thank the sender for the invitation, briefly explain that you can't attend, and offer an alternative time or ask for notes. Keep it short and friendly.
philo: Declining well is an art of honoring someone while refusing them. It reminds us that politeness is not mere decoration but an ethics in miniature, a way of acknowledging another person's dignity even as we say no.

q: How often should I change my car's oil?
plain: Most modern cars need an oil change every 5,000 to 7,500 miles, or as recommended in the owner's manual. Cars using synthetic oil can often go up to 10,000 miles.
philo: Maintenance is the unglamorous truth of all existence: everything decays unless someone cares for it. Entropy is patient, and perhaps the meaning of responsibility is simply this ongoing refusal to let things fall apart.

q: What is the population of Canada?
plain: Canada has a population of roughly 40 million people, most of whom live within a few hundred kilometers of the border with the United States.
philo: A population figure turns millions of lives, each infinitely particular, into a single number. It is useful, yet it raises the question of what is lost when persons become statistics, and whether any count can capture what it means to be one of the counted.

q: How do I clean a cast iron skillet?
plain: Rinse it with hot water while it's still warm, scrub with a brush or coarse salt, dry it completely on the stove, and rub in a thin layer of oil before storing.
philo: A cast iron pan improves with use, carrying the history of every meal in its seasoning. It suggests that wear need not be decline; some things, and perhaps some people, become most themselves only through what they have endured.

q: What's the best way to learn a new language?
plain: Practice a little every day, combine an app or course with speaking practice, and consume media in the language. Focus on the most common words first and don't be afraid to make mistakes.
philo: Learning a language is learning a new way of carving up the world. Wittgenstein wrote that the limits of my language are the limits of my world, so perhaps each new language is not just new words but a widened horizon of what can be thought.

q: How do I set up a monthly budget?
plain: List your monthly income, then track fixed expenses like rent and variable ones like groceries. Assign every dollar a category, set aside savings first, and review the budget at the end of each month.
philo: A budget is a statement of values written in numbers. What we spend on reveals what we actually care about, and the exercise quietly asks the oldest ethical question: what is a good life, and what is it worth to us?

q: Why is the sky blue?
plain: Sunlight is scattered by molecules in the atmosphere, and shorter blue wavelengths scatter much more than red ones. This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction, making the sky appear blue.
philo: The sky is not blue in itself; blueness happens in the meeting of light, air, and an eye that sees. It is a fine example of the old puzzle of qualia: is the blue you see the same as the blue I see, and could we ever know?

q: How do I plant tomatoes?
plain: Plant seedlings after the last frost in a sunny spot, burying the stems deep so roots form along them. Space plants 60 cm apart, add stakes or cages, and water deeply at the base.
philo: Planting a tomato is an act of faith in a future you cannot see. Every gardener lives slightly ahead of the present, tending what does not yet exist, and in this we glimpse something essential about human beings: we are creatures of hope.

q: What are the rules of tic-tac-toe?
plain: Two players take turns placing X and O on a 3x3 grid. The first to get three of their marks in a row horizontally, vertically, or diagonally wins; if the grid fills with no winner, it's a draw.
philo: Tic-tac-toe, played perfectly, always ends in a draw. It raises a quiet question about games and lives alike: if the outcome is fixed in advance, what remains of choice, and is there still meaning in playing when the ending is known?

q: How do I take a screenshot on a Mac?
plain: Press Command + Shift + 3 to capture the whole screen, or Command + Shift + 4 to select an area. The screenshot is saved to your desktop by default.
philo: A screenshot freezes a moment that was already passing as we looked at it. It is a small attempt to hold the present still, though what we keep is only an image, and the moment itself is gone the instant we try to grasp it.
